summary: This informational document describes the framework of the Simplified Use of Policy Abstractions (SUPA) working group. It defines base YANG data models for expressing policy, which point to device-, technology- and service-specific models developed elsewhere. The idea is that an operator can write policy rules at a high level and have them applied to many kinds of network equipment.

eli5.summary: Instead of telling every robot exactly what to do, you write one set of house rules in simple words. This is a way to write such rules for network equipment.

subtitle: Write high-level network policies once, apply them across all equipment.

tldr.problem: Network operators manage equipment from many vendors, each with different configuration interfaces and languages. Writing policies that apply consistently across a diverse infrastructure requires translating the same intent into many vendor-specific formats.
tldr.mechanism: SUPA (Simplified Use of Policy Abstractions) defines a Generic Policy Information Model (GPIM) and an Event-Condition-Action Policy Rule model (EPRIM) that operators translate into YANG data models. These abstract models can be mapped to any vendor's equipment without rewriting the policy logic.
tldr.outcome: Operators can write network policies at a high level and have them applied consistently across heterogeneous infrastructure, reducing manual configuration work and improving consistency.

today: RFC 8328 is an Informational RFC from the Independent Submission stream published in March 2018. It describes the conceptual framework for policy management; related RFCs define the actual YANG data models (like the Generic Policy Data Model) and application scenarios.

sections.title: The Problem: Policy Everywhere, Format Nowhere
sections.content:
Large networks consist of routers, switches, firewalls, and load balancers from different vendors. Network operators want to express a single policy—'block DNS queries from this subnet,' or 'migrate services when a user moves'—and have it applied consistently to all equipment.

Today, that is difficult. Each vendor's equipment has its own configuration language. What is a rule in one vendor's CLI might be a different construct in another's API. Operators must either manually translate policies for each device, or accept inconsistency.

SUPA addresses this by providing a framework for writing policies in a vendor-independent language, then mapping those policies to vendor-specific configuration.
sections.eli5: When you have many different robots, you want to tell them all the same rule without learning each robot's language. SUPA provides a way to do that.

sections.title: The SUPA Layers: From Abstract to Concrete
sections.content:
SUPA defines a stack of models that move from abstract concepts to concrete implementations:

Generic Policy Information Model (GPIM): This is the highest-level, most abstract representation. It defines policy concepts like rules, conditions, and actions without being tied to any specific technology or protocol. It is a vocabulary and framework that can be used to discuss policies independent of their implementation.

ECA Policy Rule Information Model (EPRIM): This refines the GPIM by defining a specific structure: Event-Condition-Action. A policy is a rule that triggers on an event (e.g., a link becomes congested), checks a condition (is this the peak hour?), and executes an action (route traffic away). This is still technology-agnostic; it just specifies the rule structure.

Generic Policy Data Models (GPDM): These are concrete YANG modules derived from the GPIM and EPRIM. YANG is a data modeling language used to configure network devices via NETCONF. At this level, the abstract policy concepts are mapped to actual data structures that devices can understand.
sections.eli5: Layer 1 is 'what is a rule?' (abstract). Layer 2 is 'when does it trigger and what does it do?' (less abstract). Layer 3 is 'here is the exact format my equipment understands' (concrete).

sections.title: How Operators and Equipment Interact
sections.content:
An operator writes a policy using SUPA's generic models. For example, 'if device CPU exceeds 80 percent, then reduce the number of flows it handles' is expressed in the EPRIM.

This policy is then translated into one or more YANG modules, which are sent to a network controller, orchestrator, or element management system (EMS). The controller understands the operator's intent (reduce load) and applies it to the equipment under its control.

The key benefit is that the operator never writes vendor-specific code. Instead, the operator expresses intent in SUPA's unified language, and the management system translates that intent to whatever format each piece of equipment requires.

SUPA also defines how policies relate to other management data. Policies control resources (like bandwidth allocation) and services (like VPN configurations). This enables a single policy to coordinate across multiple layers of network infrastructure.
sections.eli5: The operator says 'do this' in simple words. The management system translates it to each vendor's format. The equipment does what the operator asked.

sections.title: Consistency, Scalability, and Reuse
sections.content:
SUPA's abstraction layer provides several advantages:

Consistency: The same policy applies to all equipment, reducing the risk of configuration errors or inconsistencies that could create security holes or performance problems.

Scalability: As networks grow, operators do not need to rewrite policies for new equipment or new vendors. The SUPA framework handles the translation.

Reuse: A policy written for one network can be adapted for another without rewriting. The abstract nature of the GPIM makes policies portable across different technologies.

Interoperability: Vendors can implement SUPA support in their management systems, allowing policies to work across heterogeneous infrastructure without vendor lock-in.
sections.eli5: Write once, apply everywhere. Update once, every device follows. Simple rules that work with any vendor.
